parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how speed and velocity are different - one only tells you how fast, the other also tells you something about direction and position change.
parts.proper_answer: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Speed Is Not Enough**
You already know speed tells you how fast something moves. Velocity is the vector version of that. A vector needs both magnitude and direction, so you need to link the motion to a change in position in a particular direction.

Step 2: **Use Displacement For Direction**
In physics the directed change in position is called displacement, $s$. So velocity $v$ is defined by $$v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$$ That is, change in displacement per unit time, or rate of change of displacement.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A student throws a ball over a vertical wall of height $h$, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

The ball leaves the hand of the student at a height of $1.2\text{ m}$ above the horizontal ground. The ball has an initial velocity of $22\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $40^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The wall is a horizontal distance of $36\text{ m}$ from where the student releases the ball.

Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Determine the time taken for the ball to reach the wall.
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on the horizontal journey to the wall. With air resistance negligible, what is the horizontal acceleration and what does that tell you about horizontal speed?
Hint 2: Resolve the 22 m s-1 launch velocity into its horizontal part using the 40 degree angle, then use constant-speed distance divided by speed to get the time.
parts.proper_answer: Horizontal velocity $= 22\cos40^{\circ} = 17\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Time $= 36 / (22\cos40^{\circ}) = 2.1\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Horizontal From Vertical**
A projectile is really two independent motions. Vertically it accelerates down at $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Horizontally there is no force if air resistance is negligible, so horizontal acceleration is zero and horizontal velocity stays constant.

Step 2: **Find The Horizontal Component**
Only part of the $22\text{ m s}^{-1}$ points horizontally. The angle to the horizontal is $40^{\circ}$, so the adjacent side of the triangle is cosine: $$v_x = 22 \cos40^{\circ}$$ $$v_x \approx 16.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This stays the same all the way to the wall.

Step 3: **Time From Constant Speed**
For uniform motion, distance = speed $\times$ time. The wall is $36\text{ m}$ away horizontally: $$t = \frac{36}{v_x} = \frac{36}{22\cos40^{\circ}}$$ $$t \approx 2.1\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the vertical component $u$ of the initial velocity of the ball.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the same velocity triangle again - this time you want the side opposite the 40 degree angle, pointing straight up.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick Out The Vertical Side**
The launch velocity points up at $40^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The vertical part is the opposite side of the right-angled triangle, so you use sine: $$u = 22 \sin40^{\circ}$$ $$u \approx 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is the initial upward speed you will use in the vertical equations of motion.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The ball just goes over the wall.

Calculate the height $h$ of the wall.

markscheme_points.text: other methods possible e.g. time to maximum height = (0 − 14) / −9.81 (= 1.43 s) time from maximum height to wall = 2.1 − 1.43 (= 0.67 s) maximum height above release = (14 × 1.43) + (½ × −9.81 × 1.43²) = 9.99 (m)
height from maximum to wall = 0.5 × 9.81 × 0.67² (= 2.2 m) height above release = 9.99 − 2.2 = 7.8 (m)

hints: Hint 1: Now switch to vertical motion only. List what you know: initial upward velocity u from (ii), time t from (i), and downward acceleration g.
Hint 2: Think about which SUVAT equation links s, u, a and t when you do not know the final velocity at the wall.
Hint 3: Remember the s you calculate is measured from the release point, not from the ground - check Fig. 2.1 to see what must be added to get h.
parts.proper_answer: Vertical rise above release $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2} = 7.8\text{ m}$. Height of wall $h = 7.8 + 1.2 = 9.0\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up Vertical SUVAT**
Take upwards as positive. Then $u \approx 14.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $a = -g = -9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ because gravity pulls down, and $t \approx 2.14\text{ s}$ from (i). You want the vertical displacement $s$ from the hand to the top of the wall.

Step 2: **Apply s = ut + 1/2 at^2**
Final velocity at the wall is unknown, so use: $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ $$s = (14.1 \times 2.14) + \frac{1}{2} \times (-9.81) \times (2.14)^{2}$$ The first term is about $+30.2\text{ m}$ upward, the second is about $-22.4\text{ m}$ due to gravity. So $$s \approx 7.8\text{ m}$$ This means the ball is 7.8 m above the hand when it is over the wall.

Step 3: **Add The Release Height**
The hand started $1.2\text{ m}$ above the ground, so the height above ground is: $$h = s + 1.2$$ $$h \approx 7.8 + 1.2 = 9.0\text{ m}$$ That is just enough to clear the wall.
